sections.html:
Probate is the court process that settles a dead person's affairs. A personal representative gathers the property, pays valid debts and expenses, and hands what is left to the people entitled to it. When there is a valid will, the estate is distributed under it. Without one, Illinois inheritance law decides who gets what. The representative named in a will is the executor. When there is no will, the court appoints an administrator.

The case opens in the circuit court of the county where the decedent lived. An Illinois lawyer must file it. The estate is its own legal entity and can't represent itself, so a family member who tries to file alone will be told to hire counsel.

sections.h2: When a house has to go through probate
sections.html:
Probate is usually needed when the person owned real estate in their own name alone and nothing moves it automatically at death. A house held in joint tenancy with survivorship, held in a trust, or covered by a recorded Transfer on Death Instrument passes outside probate. A will by itself doesn't avoid it, because the court still has to appoint the executor and give that person authority.

A jointly owned home normally becomes the surviving spouse's property. If the house stood only in the deceased spouse's name, probate may still be needed. The title company decides what it needs to insure a sale, so ask early which documents it will accept.

  • Sole name, no beneficiary designation: probate is usually required.
  • Joint tenancy with survivorship: passes to the surviving owner.
  • Trust or Transfer on Death Instrument: follows the instrument.

sections.h2: Steps from filing to closing the estate
sections.html:
The lawyer files a petition in the right county. When there is a will, the petition asks the court to admit it and name the executor, and the court won't look at the petition until the will itself is on file. Whoever holds a will must file it with the clerk right after death. Once the court is satisfied, it appoints the representative and issues letters of office.

After that come notices to creditors, collecting and protecting the property, paying debts and expenses, and distribution. Illinois has no single statewide set of forms, so the circuit clerk of the county supplies the petitions and notices.

Core Illinois probate rules that affect a house sale.
StepRuleStatute section
File the willWhoever holds it files it with the circuit clerk right after death5/6-1
Creditor noticePublish once a week for 3 successive weeks in a newspaper of the county and mail known creditors5/18-3
Claims deadline in the noticeAt least 6 months from first publication, or 3 months from mailing, whichever is later5/18-3
Outside limit on claimsBarred 2 years after death even if no letters issue5/18-12(b)
Independent administrationRepresentative acts without court orders unless the Article or an interested person requires them5/28-1

Under Article 28, an executor or administrator can run the estate without court orders or filings, except where the Article or an interested person asks for the court to step in. An independent representative acting reasonably for the estate's best interests may lease, mortgage or sell the decedent's real estate at public or private sale, for cash or on credit, without asking the judge.

One limit matters for a sale. Real estate that the will specifically leaves to a named person can't be leased, sold or mortgaged without that person's written consent. A representative can also confirm title in an heir or legatee by recording an instrument that releases the estate's interest.

Any interested person can petition to end independent status. The court must grant the petition unless the will directs independent administration, in which case it needs good cause, or unless the petitioner is a creditor or a legatee other than a residuary legatee, in which case the court must find that termination is necessary to protect that person. After termination, the representative follows the rules for supervised administration.

sections.h2: Creditor claims and the timing of a sale
sections.html:
Creditors get a set window to file. The published notice names a claim date no earlier than six months after first publication, or three months after the notice is mailed or delivered, whichever is later. A claim not filed by that date is barred, and in any event all claims are barred two years after death.

A representative who gives proper notice in good faith isn't personally liable to a creditor. A claim that isn't barred can still be pursued against assets not yet distributed, and against a distributee up to the amount that person received above what they would have gotten had the claim been paid. The bar doesn't cut off actions to establish the decedent's liability to the extent liability insurance covers it.

A person who dies without a valid will is intestate, and Illinois law picks the heirs. Property may go to a surviving spouse, children, parents or other relatives as the statute lays out, which can differ from what the person would have chosen. The court names an administrator with the same duties as an executor: collect assets, pay debts and expenses, and distribute the rest.

If you find a will after the case starts, take it to the lawyer at once and file it with the clerk. The Probate Act makes it a Class 3 felony to willfully alter or destroy a will without the testator's direction, or to hide one for 30 days after learning of the death.

  • Locate the original will, not a copy.
  • Ask the title company what proof of authority it wants, since title companies often need to see the letters of office.
  • Keep a list of every parcel the decedent owned, because each deed may need its own recording.

sections.h2: Can a small estate skip probate?
sections.html:
Some estates can, but a house rules out the shortcut. A small estate affidavit works only if the estate has no real estate, at least 60 days must go by after the death, no probate petition is filed or pending, and total personal property is $150,000 or less. Registered motor vehicles are listed on the affidavit but don't count toward the cap.

Under 755 ILCS 5/25-1 the affiant must also pay valid claims before distributing to heirs. The affidavit transfers personal property such as accounts, not land. A homeowner heir should plan on a probate case, a trust, a Transfer on Death Instrument or joint title to move a house.

  • Check how the deed reads before assuming probate is needed.
  • Ask the circuit clerk in the county of death for forms and local steps.
  • Illinois Legal Aid Online offers a free application for people who can't afford a lawyer.

Many heirs want to sell rather than keep the property. Start by asking the lawyer whether the representative has letters of office and independent status. Then pull together the death certificate, the deed, the latest tax bill and any mortgage statement for the title company.

Plan on the court timeline, not the buyer's, setting the pace. A cash sale doesn't wait on a lender's appraisal or loan approval, so once the representative can sign, closing can move quickly.

faqs.q: Do I need a lawyer to open probate in Illinois?
faqs.a: Yes. An Illinois lawyer must open the case, and the court will pause one filed by a family member until counsel is found.

faqs.q: Can an executor sell the house during probate?
faqs.a: Often yes. An independent representative may sell real estate without a court order under 755 ILCS 5/28-8, but property specifically left to a legatee needs that person's written consent.

faqs.q: How long do creditors have to file claims?
faqs.a: The notice sets a date at least six months after first publication or three months after mailing, whichever is later. All claims are barred two years after death regardless of letters (755 ILCS 5/18-3 and 18-12).

faqs.q: Does a will avoid probate in Illinois?
faqs.a: No. A will names who gets the property and often names the executor, but if the property must pass through probate the court still appoints the executor and gives that person authority.

faqs.q: Which court handles an Illinois probate case?
faqs.a: The circuit court in the county where the decedent lived. Forms and filing steps differ by county, so start with the circuit clerk's office or website.
